edition: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – testable section (Parts 1–4), current resource book (2020 edition, updated 2024 to name King Charles III); values-test format in force since 15 November 2020

exam.rules: A computer-based multiple-choice test in English with 20 randomly selected questions drawn from the testable section (Parts 1–4) of Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond, taken in 45 minutes. Five of the 20 questions are about Australian values. To pass you must answer ALL 5 Australian values questions correctly AND score at least 75% overall (15 of 20). Getting any values question wrong is a fail even with 15 or more correct. In this app, values questions have topic "values"; a mock exam draws 5 values questions plus 15 from the other topics.

questions.q: Who were Australia's first inhabitants?
options: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
questions.explain: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples were the first inhabitants and have the oldest continuous cultures in the world.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 1: Australia and its people (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples)

questions.q: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have what distinction among the world's cultures?
options: The oldest continuous cultures and traditions in the world
The youngest cultures in the world
questions.explain: Their cultures are the oldest continuous cultures in the world.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 1: Australia and its people (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples)

questions.q: According to the archaeological record, when did Aboriginal peoples arrive in Australia?
questions.explain: The archaeological record indicates arrival between 65,000 and 40,000 years ago.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 1: Australia and its people (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples)

questions.q: Where are Torres Strait Islander people from?
options: Islands between the northern tip of Queensland and Papua New Guinea
Islands off the coast of Western Australia

questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 1: Australia and its people (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples)

questions.q: Historically, where are Aboriginal people from?
questions.explain: Aboriginal people are historically from mainland Australia and Tasmania.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 1: Australia and its people (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples)

questions.explain: Their connection to the land is expressed in stories, art and dance.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 1: Australia and its people (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples)

questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 1: Australia and its people (Early days of European settlement)

questions.q: How many ships were in the First Fleet?
questions.explain: The First Fleet was made up of 11 ships.

questions.q: Who was the first Governor of the colony of New South Wales?
questions.explain: Captain Arthur Phillip led the First Fleet and was the first Governor of NSW.

questions.q: Why did the British Government send convicts to New South Wales?
options: British jails were too full to hold all the prisoners
questions.explain: British laws were harsh and jails were overcrowded, so convicts were transported to the new colony.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 1: Australia and its people (Early days of European settlement)

questions.q: Who were the people on the first ships that arrived in 1788?
questions.explain: The First Fleet carried convicts to establish the colony of New South Wales.

questions.q: Early free settlers in Australia came mainly from which countries?

questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 1: Australia and its people (Early days of European settlement)

questions.q: In what year did a gold rush begin in New South Wales and Victoria?

questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 1: Australia and its people (Early days of European settlement)

questions.q: During the gold rush, which group became the first large group of migrants not from Europe?

questions.q: What happened to Australia's population in the 10 years after the gold rush began?

questions.q: In what year were the separate colonies united into a federation called the Commonwealth of Australia?

questions.q: Under Australian law, can two men or two women marry each other?
questions.explain: Under Australian law, two people can marry, including two men or two women.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Equality of all people under the law)

questions.q: Which of these rights do both men and women have in Australia?
options: Only men can stand for parliament
Only men can join the police
Only women can apply for divorce
To vote, stand for parliament and join the Defence Force and police
questions.explain: Men and women have equal access to education, employment, voting, parliament, the ADF and the police.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Equality of all people under the law)

questions.q: In Australia, can a woman get a job ahead of a man if she has better qualifications and skills?
options: No, men must be given priority
questions.explain: It is a woman's right to get a job ahead of a man if she has better qualifications and skills.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Equality of all people under the law)

questions.q: Who can make independent choices about personal matters such as marriage and religion?
questions.explain: Both men and women can make their own independent choices about personal matters.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Equality of all people under the law)

questions.q: Is physical violence against a spouse or partner ever acceptable in Australia?
options: Yes, if it is a cultural practice
No, it is a criminal offence
questions.explain: Physical violence against a spouse or partner is never acceptable and is a criminal offence.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Equality of all people under the law)

questions.q: Is divorce acceptable in Australia?
options: Yes, either a husband or a wife may apply
questions.explain: Divorce is acceptable; either spouse may apply even if the other wants to stay married.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Equality of all people under the law)

questions.q: Can a wife apply for a divorce even if her husband wants to continue the marriage?
questions.explain: Either a husband or a wife may apply for divorce, even if the other spouse wishes to continue the marriage.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Equality of all people under the law)

questions.q: When an organisation fills a job, whom does the law support it in selecting?
options: The person with the best skills and experience
The person from the largest ethnic group
questions.explain: The law supports selecting the person with the best skills and experience.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Equality of opportunity and a 'fair go')

questions.q: What should a person's achievements in life be based on?
questions.explain: What someone achieves should result from their hard work and talents.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Equality of opportunity and a 'fair go')

questions.q: Should a person get a job because of their gender, wealth or ethnicity?
options: No, it should be based on skills and experience
questions.explain: Jobs should be given on skills and experience, not gender, wealth or ethnicity.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Equality of opportunity and a 'fair go')

questions.q: Is there a formal class system in Australian society?
options: No; people should not be limited by class distinctions
questions.explain: Australians believe everyone deserves a fair go, without class distinctions.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Equality of opportunity and a 'fair go')

questions.q: Is violence of any kind, including verbal and physical abuse, legal in Australia?
questions.explain: Violence of any kind, including verbal and physical abuse, is illegal.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Mutual respect and tolerance)

questions.q: How do Australians believe disagreements should be handled?
options: Peacefully, respecting the right of all to be safe from violence and intimidation
questions.explain: Australians believe in peaceful disagreement and the right to be safe from violence and intimidation.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Mutual respect and tolerance)

questions.q: What is the age of sexual consent in Australia?
options: 16 or 17, depending on the state or territory
questions.explain: The age of consent is 16 or 17 depending on the state or territory.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Mutual respect and tolerance)

questions.q: A 20-year-old man wants to have sexual relations with a 15-year-old girl. Is this legal in Australia?
options: No, it is against the law in all states and territories
questions.explain: It is illegal in all Australian states and territories.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Mutual respect and tolerance)

questions.q: Should you obey a lawful request from the police?
options: Only if a lawyer is present
Yes, because Australians commit to following the law
questions.explain: Lawful actions of the police should be supported, and you should obey a lawful request.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Mutual respect and tolerance)

questions.q: What does mutual respect and tolerance mean?
options: Listening to others and respecting their views even when they differ from yours
Only respecting people of your own culture
questions.explain: It means listening to and respecting others' views and being tolerant where you disagree.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Mutual respect and tolerance)

questions.q: Is it acceptable to make racially abusive comments at a sporting event?
options: No, racism has no place in Australia
Yes, if it is a joke
Yes, if the other team started it
Yes, it is part of sport
questions.explain: Racism has no place in Australia, including racially abusive comments in public or at sporting events.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Mutual respect and tolerance)

questions.q: Is it acceptable to create or share racially offensive material on the internet?
options: Yes, if it is a joke
questions.explain: Creating or sharing racially offensive material online is unacceptable; racism has no place in Australia.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Mutual respect and tolerance)

questions.q: Where can incidents of racism be reported?
options: To the police or the Australian Human Rights Commission
questions.explain: Racism should be reported to the police; complaints can also go to the Australian Human Rights Commission.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Glossary of testable section (racism / Australian Human Rights Commission)

questions.q: Australians expect everyone living in Australia to do what?
options: Participate in society and make a contribution to the community
questions.explain: Everyone is expected to participate and contribute to the community.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Making a contribution)

questions.q: Who has a responsibility to try to support themselves and their families when able to do so?
questions.explain: Everyone has a responsibility to try to support themselves and their families when able.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Making a contribution)

questions.q: What is 'mateship'?
options: Helping each other, especially in times of need
questions.explain: Mateship means helping and receiving help from others, especially in difficult times.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Compassion for those in need)

questions.q: Which of these is an example of mateship?
options: Driving a friend to a medical appointment
Refusing to help in a bushfire
questions.explain: Examples include taking a meal to an elderly neighbour or driving a friend to a medical appointment.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Compassion for those in need)

questions.q: What does volunteering offer people in Australia?
options: A chance to share knowledge, learn skills and feel part of the community
questions.explain: Volunteering helps people share knowledge, learn skills and integrate into the community.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Compassion for those in need)

questions.q: What is a volunteer?
options: A person who gives their time without expecting payment
questions.explain: A volunteer gives time to a person or organisation without payment.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Glossary of testable section (volunteer)

questions.q: How do Australians respond in times of crisis such as bushfires?
options: They come together and help each other
They leave it all to the government
They only help their own ethnic group
questions.explain: During the 2019-20 bushfires, many communities collected donations to help those affected.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Our community)

questions.q: How does Australian society view the English language?
options: As less important than other languages
As a language only for government
As the national language and an important unifying element
questions.explain: English is the national language and an important unifying element of society.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (English as the national language)

questions.q: Why is it important to learn English in Australia?
options: It is required to own a car
It is required to use a hospital
It helps you get an education and a job and integrate into the community
It is needed to practise religion
questions.explain: English helps with education, employment and integration and is essential for social cohesion.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (English as the national language)

questions.q: What must applicants for Australian citizenship undertake to do if English is not their native language?
options: Make reasonable efforts to learn English
questions.explain: Applicants must undertake to make reasonable efforts to learn English.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (English as the national language)

questions.q: If you suspect a neighbour is planning a serious crime, what should you do?
options: Report it to Australian government authorities as soon as possible
questions.explain: You should report suspected serious crimes to authorities as soon as possible.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Helping to keep our society safe)

questions.q: If you see or know of a child being abused, what should you do?
options: Post about it on social media
questions.explain: Child abuse should be reported to the police to investigate.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Helping to keep our society safe)

questions.q: What is cyber abuse?
options: Using technology to threaten, intimidate, harass or humiliate someone
Using the internet to pay bills
questions.explain: Cyber abuse is behaviour using technology to threaten, harass or humiliate; many forms are illegal.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Helping to keep our society safe) / Glossary

questions.q: Which of these is an example of cyber abuse?
options: Posting a holiday photo of yourself
Sharing sexual photos of someone online without their consent
questions.explain: Sharing sexual images without consent, online stalking and racist abuse online are examples of cyber abuse.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Helping to keep our society safe)

questions.q: Is online abuse accepted in Australia?
options: Yes, online speech has no limits
No, and many forms are illegal
questions.explain: Online abuse is not accepted, and many forms are illegal.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Helping to keep our society safe)

questions.q: Can an Australian citizen hold citizenship of another country?
options: Yes, if the laws of the other country allow it
questions.explain: Dual or multiple citizenship is possible if the other country's laws allow it.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Loyalty to Australia)

questions.q: Must a dual citizen in Australia obey all Australian laws?
options: No, they can choose which country's laws to follow
Only if they were born in Australia
questions.explain: Even dual citizens in Australia must follow all Australian laws at all times.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Loyalty to Australia)

questions.q: Do some Australian laws apply to Australian citizens even when they are overseas?
options: Yes, for example laws against sexual activity with a child under 16
No, Australian law never applies overseas
questions.explain: Some laws apply overseas; it is illegal for Australians to engage in sexual activity with a child under 16 anywhere.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Loyalty to Australia)

questions.q: Which of these would undermine Australia's interests?
options: Using social media to share official government secrets
questions.explain: Sharing official government secrets on social media undermines Australia's interests.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Loyalty to Australia)

questions.q: Which of these would damage Australian community relations?
options: Promoting distrust and fear of an ethnic community
questions.explain: Promoting distrust of an ethnic community damages community relations.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Loyalty to Australia)

questions.q: In the citizenship pledge, to whom do Australian citizens pledge loyalty?
questions.explain: Citizens pledge loyalty to Australia and its people.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Loyalty to Australia)

questions.q: Should all people in Australia be given equal opportunity to pursue their goals regardless of ethnicity or religion?
options: Yes, as long as they obey Australian law
questions.explain: All people should have equal opportunity regardless of ethnicity or religion, as long as they obey the law.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Freedom of religion)

questions.q: What must religious practices in Australia not do?
questions.explain: Religious practices must not break Australian laws.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Freedom of religion)

questions.q: Is it a right of people in Australia to be safe from violence and intimidation?
questions.explain: Australians believe above all in the right to be safe and free from violence and intimidation.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Mutual respect and tolerance)

questions.q: Which values are a reason so many people want to become Australian citizens?
options: Australian values that define and shape the country
questions.explain: The guide states Australian values define the country and are a reason people want to become citizens.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values

questions.q: What does Australian citizenship ask you to do with Australian values?
options: Respect, share and uphold them in everyday life
Follow them only when in public
Keep them only in mind during ceremonies
Replace them with your own laws
questions.explain: Citizenship is about living out these values in everyday life and in your community.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values

questions.q: Is it acceptable to discriminate against someone at work because they are a woman?
options: Yes, if it is a tradition
No, it is against the law
questions.explain: It is against the law to discriminate against a person because of their gender.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Equality of all people under the law)

questions.q: How are people from different backgrounds treated under Australian law?
options: Neither given preferential treatment nor discriminated against
Citizens by birth receive more rights
questions.explain: The law ensures people from different backgrounds are neither preferred nor discriminated against.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Equality of all people under the law)

questions.q: Are Australians free to join or leave any lawful group voluntarily?
questions.explain: People are free to join or leave any group voluntarily, within the law.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Freedom of association)

questions.q: Must other people's freedom of speech be respected, as long as their expression is lawful?
options: No, only your own freedom matters
Only if you agree with them
questions.explain: Other people's lawful freedom of speech and expression must be respected.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Freedom of speech)

questions.q: Many new migrants have become leaders in business, the arts and sport. According to the guide, how did they achieve this?
questions.explain: Many migrants have become leaders through hard work and enterprise.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values (Equality of opportunity and a 'fair go')

questions.q: If a person's cultural practice is different from Australian law, what must they do?
options: Ask a religious leader to decide
questions.explain: Regardless of background or culture, you must follow Australian laws.
questions.ref: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond – Part 4: Australian values
